q.q: What is a database?
o: A single spreadsheet of numbers that is mainly used to carry out calculations
An organised collection of related data that can be searched, sorted and presented
A program that controls the computer's hardware and shares out its resources
A printed list of records that has been grouped and sorted by one field
q.why: A database organises related data so it can be searched, sorted and presented quickly.

q.q: In a database table, what is one column called?
o: A field
A record
A table
A query
q.why: A field is one item of data stored for every record, shown as a column. A record is a row.

q.q: In a hockey club's Members table, two sisters are both called Doherty. Why is Surname a poor key field?
o: Two members can share the same surname, so it is not unique
Surnames are stored as text, and text cannot be a key
Surnames are too long to be typed in quickly and accurately
Surnames can be sorted into alphabetical order by a query
q.why: A key field must be unique for every record; surnames can repeat.

q.q: Which two rules must a key field follow?
o: It must be a number and be the first field in the table
It must be unique and always use the AutoNumber data type
It must be unique for every record and never be left blank
It must mix letters with digits and be under 8 characters
q.why: A primary key identifies exactly one record, so it must be unique and never blank. AutoNumber is common but not required.

q.q: What is a composite key?
o: A key field from another table used to link the tables
A field that holds a mix of letters and numbers
A key field whose values are created automatically
Two fields used together to identify each record uniquely
q.why: When no single field is unique, two fields together can form a composite key. A key from another table is a foreign key.

q.q: A table records which members played in each match. Why might MemberID plus MatchDate be used as the key?
o: MemberID alone is unique in every table it appears in
MatchDate alone is unique because no two matches are alike
Neither field alone is unique, but together they are
Two fields together always make the database run faster
q.why: A member plays in many matches and many members play on one date, but each pair appears once.

q.q: What is a flat file database?
o: A database that splits its data into several linked tables
A table that has been created without any key field
A database that stores all of its data in a single table
A plain text file that has no formatting of any kind
q.why: Flat means one two-dimensional table holds everything.

q.q: In a flat-file bookings table, the Doherty family's surname and phone number are typed on every one of their booking rows. Which problem is this?
o: Referential integrity
Data redundancy
Data portability
Validation
q.why: Redundancy is the same data stored many times, wasting space and typing time.

q.q: The Dohertys change their phone number, but only one of their rows in a flat file is updated. Which problem results?
o: Inconsistency: the file now holds two different numbers for one family
Redundancy: the new number is moved into a separate linked table
Referential integrity: the booking is rejected by the database
Validation: the new number fails a range check and is refused
q.why: Because data is repeated, updating one copy and not the others leaves conflicting values.

q.q: How does a relational database reduce data redundancy?
o: All the data is kept in one table so nothing needs repeating
Each fact is stored once and tables are linked by relationships
Repeated data is compressed so that it uses less space
Each table is given two primary keys instead of one
q.why: Member details are stored once in Members; Bookings only hold the MemberID link.

q.q: For which of these would a flat file be suitable?
o: Members and their many bookings
Pupils who each study many subjects
A simple contacts list
Library books and the loans of each one
q.why: Flat files are fine for simple lists; linked data such as one member with many bookings needs a relational database.

q.q: Why can retyping the same details on many rows of a flat file cause searches to miss records?
o: Flat files cannot be searched by any field that contains text values
Errors such as a misspelt surname creep in each time the data is retyped
Each retyped row is automatically stored in a different table
Searches only look at the first row of a flat file database
q.why: A misspelt copy no longer matches the search, so that record is missed.

q.q: What is a foreign key?
o: The second key field that every table in a database must have
A field whose values must be unique within its own table
A field in one table that holds values of another table's primary key
A key made from two fields that are used together
q.why: The foreign key provides the link to the table where that field is the primary key.

q.q: Why can the same value appear many times in a foreign key field?
o: The database does not check foreign key values against anything
Foreign key fields always use the AutoNumber data type
Each table is allowed to have several primary keys
One record in the first table can link to many records in the second
q.why: HK101 can appear on many bookings because one member makes many bookings.

q.q: A library database has Books(BookID, Title, Author) and Loans(LoanID, BookID, PupilID, DateOut). What is the primary key of Loans?
o: BookID
LoanID
PupilID
DateOut
q.why: LoanID identifies each loan uniquely. BookID repeats in Loans because one book is borrowed many times.

q.q: A library database has Books(BookID, Title, Author) and Loans(LoanID, BookID, PupilID, DateOut). Which field in Loans links it to Books?
o: LoanID
PupilID
BookID
DateOut
q.why: BookID is the primary key of Books, stored in Loans as a foreign key.

q.q: What must be true of the common field before two tables can be linked?
o: It must have the same data type in both tables
It must be the primary key in both tables
It must hold unique values in both tables
It must have the same validation rule in both tables
q.why: Linked fields must have matching data types, e.g. both Short Text. It is the primary key in one table only.

q.q: On an Access relationship line, what is shown at the primary key end?
o: A crow's foot
M
q.why: The line shows 1 at the primary key ('one') end and ∞ at the foreign key ('many') end.

q.q: A pupil says a foreign key is 'the second key field of a table'. What is the correct description?
o: A second primary key that is unique in its table and is used as a backup key
A normal field in its table that happens to hold another table's primary key values
A field that is never used for linking but stores a copy of the key field
A field whose values are created automatically by AutoNumber in each table
q.why: The notes warn against 'second key field'; the foreign key is a non-key field holding another table's key values.

q.q: Each pupil has one locker and each locker belongs to one pupil. Which relationship is this?
o: One-to-many
One-to-one
Many-to-many
No relationship
q.why: Each record in one table links to exactly one record in the other, and vice versa.

q.q: One doctor has many patients, and each patient has one doctor. How is this relationship best described?
o: One-to-many, with Patients on the 'one' side
One-to-one, because each patient has one doctor
One-to-many, with Doctors on the 'one' side
Many-to-many, because there are many patients
q.why: Name the 'one' side first: one doctor has many patients.

q.q: How is a many-to-many relationship normally built in a database?
o: By adding a link table to make two one-to-many relationships
By linking the two primary keys directly to each other
By switching on referential integrity for both tables
By storing both tables together in one flat file
q.why: A link table such as Enrolments(PupilID, SubjectID) turns it into two one-to-many relationships.

q.q: What is the purpose of referential integrity?
o: To make sure every field has been given the correct data type
To check that data has been copied accurately from paper forms
To stop the same field name from appearing in two tables
To keep linked tables consistent so there are no orphan records
q.why: Foreign keys must match an existing primary key, so no record links to nothing.

q.q: Referential integrity is enforced without cascade delete. A user tries to delete member HK101, who still has bookings. What happens?
o: HK101 and all of their bookings are deleted together
HK101 is deleted and their bookings are left behind
The bookings are moved across to another member
The deletion is refused while bookings still point to HK101
q.why: Deleting the member would leave orphan bookings, so it is not allowed.

q.q: Cascade delete is switched on. A member who has bookings is deleted. What happens to the bookings?
o: They stop the member from being deleted
They are deleted along with the member
They remain as orphan records
They are moved to a new table
q.why: Cascade delete removes linked records when the 'one' record is deleted.

q.q: What is an orphan record?
o: A record that has been left without any primary key value
A record that appears twice in the same database table
A record whose foreign key links to a record that does not exist
A record that has not yet been included in a backup
q.why: Referential integrity exists to stop records pointing to nothing.

q.q: Which database tool searches the tables and extracts only the records that meet set criteria?
o: Form
Report
Macro
Query
q.why: A query finds and extracts matching records. A report presents data but does not search.

q.q: What is the purpose of a report?
o: To search the tables and pick out the matching records
To present data in a formatted layout for printing or on screen
To enter or edit new records, usually one at a time
To carry out a series of actions automatically
q.why: Reports present data neatly, often grouped, sorted and totalled.

q.q: How can a form help to keep data accurate?
o: It can limit what is typed, for example with drop-down lists
It searches the table for duplicate records and removes them
It prints every record grouped by one of the fields
It stores each record twice so mistakes can be compared
q.why: Forms control input by showing only the needed fields and offering lists and buttons.

q.q: A club secretary clicks a 'Print squad list' button, which runs a query and then prints a report. What is attached to the button?
o: A field
A macro
A relationship
An import
q.why: A macro is a stored series of actions, usually attached to a button on a form.

q.q: Which statement about queries and reports is correct?
o: A report does the searching; a query presents the results
Both queries and reports are used to enter new records
A query does the searching; a report presents the results
A report can never take its data from a query
q.why: Mixing these up is a common lost mark: the query finds, the report presents.

q.q: Why do macros help staff who have little database knowledge?
o: They hide all of the tables so nothing can be changed
They check that every entry typed in is correct
One click carries out a whole series of actions for them
They remove the need for the database to have forms
q.why: Macros automate repeated tasks, saving time and reducing mistakes.

q.q: A teacher needs a printed register grouped by class and sorted by surname, with a heading and logo. Which tool produces this?
o: Query
Report
Form
Macro
q.why: Grouping, sorting and formatting for printing are the job of a report.

q.q: What does importing data into a database mean?
o: Copying data out of the database into another program
Bringing data in from another file instead of typing it again
Linking two tables using a primary key and a foreign key
Typing data into a form, one record at a time
q.why: Importing copies data in from a file such as a csv or spreadsheet. Sending data out is exporting.

q.q: In a csv file, how are the fields in each record separated?
o: By commas
By new lines
By spaces
By tabs
q.why: csv stands for comma-separated values. Each new line holds a new record.

q.q: In a csv file of new members, what does each line after the heading line represent?
o: One field
One table
One query
One record
q.why: A csv file stores one record per line, with fields separated by commas.

q.q: Before importing a csv file, what should its column headings match?
o: The record numbers in the table
The primary key values in the table
The field names in the table
The name of the csv file itself
q.why: Matching headings to field names lets each value go into the correct field.

q.q: Which is NOT a benefit of importing data?
o: It is much faster than retyping hundreds of records
It avoids transcription errors caused by retyping
Data from an online sign-up form is easily added
It guarantees that every imported value is correct
q.why: Importing saves time and avoids typing errors, but it cannot make wrong source data correct.

q.q: A row in a file being imported contains a MemberID that already exists in the table. What is likely to happen?
o: The existing member is overwritten with the new row
The whole table is deleted and rebuilt from the file
The key field type changes so both rows fit
The row is rejected or listed in an error table
q.why: The primary key must stay unique, so duplicate key values are rejected.

q.q: Which Access data type stores money values shown with two decimal places?
o: Number
Short Text
Currency
Calculated
q.why: Currency stores and displays money with two decimal places.

q.q: A field OrderID must get a new sequential number automatically for each new record. Which data type?
o: Number
Lookup Wizard
Calculated
AutoNumber
q.why: AutoNumber generates a sequential number for each new record, which suits a key field.

q.q: A field records whether a parent has given photo consent. Which data type is best?
o: Short Text
Number
Yes/No
Long Text
q.why: There are only two possible values, so a Boolean Yes/No field fits and saves space.

q.q: A field works out TotalCost from [Quantity]*[UnitPrice] in the same record. Which data type is this?
o: AutoNumber
Lookup Wizard
Calculated
Hyperlink
q.why: A Calculated field holds the result of a calculation using other fields in the same record.

q.q: A Team field lets users pick U14, U15 or U16 from a drop-down. Which data type is this?
o: Yes/No
AutoNumber
Lookup Wizard
Hyperlink
q.why: Lookup Wizard gives a list of values to choose from.

q.q: Dates are stored as text, and '02/05/2026' sorts before '15/01/2026'. Why?
o: Text sorts character by character, not in true date order
Date/Time fields always sort the newest dates first
Text fields cannot store the slash character properly
Dates must be stored as Currency to sort correctly
q.why: Stored as text, '0' comes before '1', so the dates are not in calendar order.

q.q: What is the difference between the OLE Object and Attachment data types?
o: OLE links or embeds an object made in other software; Attachment simply attaches files to a record
OLE simply attaches photos to a record; Attachment links or embeds objects made in other software
OLE stores web addresses that can be clicked; Attachment stores email addresses to send to
OLE holds the result of a calculation; Attachment holds a list of values chosen from a drop-down
q.why: Both hold files, but OLE (Object Linking and Embedding) links or embeds an object from another program.

q.q: Which is the best justification for storing a Mobile field as Short Text?
o: It starts with 0, which a Number field would drop, and it is never calculated
It is made up of numbers, so it has to be stored as some kind of text
It is short, so Short Text will use the least storage space possible
It will be added up to work out the total cost of phone calls made
q.why: A Number field drops the leading zero, and phone numbers are never used in calculations.

q.q: Which is the best justification for making SessionsAttended a Number field?
o: It is a whole number that will be totalled
It contains a mix of letters and digits
It has only two possible answers
It needs a unique value for each record
q.why: Number is for values used in calculations such as totals and averages.

q.q: Why does AutoNumber suit a CustomerID key field?
o: It lets staff type in any customer number they choose
It creates a unique value automatically for each new record
It stores money values with two decimal places
It lets the value be picked from a fixed list
q.why: A key field must be unique; AutoNumber guarantees this without anyone typing it.

q.q: Why use a Lookup Wizard for a field that only allows a fixed set of values?
o: It lets users type any value they like
Choosing from a list stops spelling mistakes
It works out the value from other fields
It stores the value as a clickable link
q.why: Picking from a list means only allowed values, spelt correctly, can be entered.

q.q: A Postcode field is set to Short Text with a field size of 8. What extra benefit does the field size give?
o: Each postcode is checked against a list of real addresses
Each postcode is changed into capital letters automatically
Over-long entries are rejected, so it acts as a length check
Postcodes can then be sorted into true date order
q.why: Setting a field size stops wasted storage and rejects entries that are too long.

q.q: Which is the best justification for storing DateJoined as Date/Time?
o: It contains a mix of letters and numbers that must be kept together
It is a money value that needs to be shown with two decimal places
It has only two possible answers, so it takes very little space
It can be sorted in date order and used to work out length of membership
q.why: Date/Time allows true date sorting and date calculations.

q.q: Who or what carries out validation?
o: The user, by reading data back against the form
A second person typing in the same data again
The database manager at the end of each day
The computer, automatically, as data is entered
q.why: Validation is an automatic check by the computer at input. Reading back and double entry are verification.

q.q: Why is validation needed?
o: It stops many input errors at the moment they are typed
It proves that all of the stored data is correct
It makes a backup copy of each new record
It encrypts the data while it is being typed
q.why: Catching errors at input is far cheaper than fixing them later, though validation cannot prove data is correct.

q.q: What is validation text?
o: The rule typed into the Validation Rule property
The error message explaining what is wrong with the entry
The list of values shown in a drop-down box
The text typed into a Short Text field
q.why: Validation text tells the user what is wrong so they can fix it.

q.q: A parent's date of birth is 21/05/1984 but is typed as 12/05/1984. Why does validation accept it?
o: Both dates are sensible, so validation cannot tell it is wrong
Validation is never carried out on any date fields
The field must have been set up as Short Text
Range checks can only be used on whole numbers
q.why: Validation checks data is allowed, not that it is correct.

q.q: Which is an example of verification?
o: Checking that the age entered is between 11 and 18
Checking that the surname field has not been left blank
Typing an email address twice so the two entries are compared
Checking that the postcode matches the pattern BT12 3AB
q.why: Double entry checks the data was entered accurately. The others are validation checks.

q.q: What is a weakness of verification by double entry?
o: Valid but wrong data is always rejected by it
If the same mistake is made twice, it still gets in
It can only be used on fields holding numbers
It checks data is within limits, not accurate
q.why: The computer only compares the two entries, so a repeated mistake matches.

q.q: Every booking must include the customer's surname. Which validation check is needed?
o: Length check
Type check
Format check
Presence check
q.why: A presence check makes sure a field is not left blank.

q.q: NumberOfNights must be a number, so 'four' should be rejected. Which check?
o: Range check
Format check
Type check
Length check
q.why: A type check makes sure the data is of the correct data type.

q.q: A membership code must be exactly 6 characters long. Which check?
o: Length check
Range check
Format check
Presence check
q.why: A length check counts characters, either an exact number or within limits.

q.q: An email address must contain the @ symbol. Which check?
o: Presence check
Type check
Format check
Length check
q.why: A format check makes sure the data matches a set pattern.

q.q: A pupil says 'NumberOfNights must be from 1 to 14' is a length check. Why is this wrong?
o: It checks a pattern of characters, so it is a format check
It compares the value with limits, so it is a range check
It checks the field is not blank, so it is a presence check
It checks the kind of data, so it is a type check
q.why: Length counts characters; range compares a value with a lower and upper limit.

q.q: How are format checks usually set up in a database?
o: Using a Lookup Wizard
Using an input mask
Using a macro
Using a composite key
q.why: An input mask sets the pattern of character types allowed in each position.

q.q: The date 31/02/2026 is typed into a Date/Time field and rejected. Which check rejected it?
o: Range check
Length check
Type check
Presence check
q.why: An impossible date is not a valid Date/Time value, so the built-in type check rejects it.

q.q: Which validation rule allows 1 to 8 passengers, including both 1 and 8?
o: >1 And <8
Len([Passengers])<=8
q.why: >= and <= include both limits. Using Or would let any number through.

q.q: Which validation rule checks that MemberCode is exactly 6 characters?
o: [MemberCode]=6
Between 1 And 6
Len([MemberCode])=6
q.why: Len counts the characters. [MemberCode]=6 compares the value itself with 6.

q.q: Which validation rule makes sure a password is at least 8 characters long?
o: Len([Password])>8
Len([Password])=8
[Password]>=8
Len([Password])>=8
q.why: 'At least 8' includes 8, so >= is needed. >8 would wrongly reject an 8-character password.

q.q: What does the validation rule Like "*@*" check?
o: The entry starts with an @ symbol
The entry is a single @ symbol only
The entry has not been left blank
The entry contains an @ symbol somewhere
q.why: The asterisks stand for any characters before and after the @, so it is a simple format check.

q.q: A field has the input mask LL0000, where L means a letter is required and 0 means a digit is required. Which entry is accepted?
o: EN204
q.why: Two letters then four digits are needed. EN204 has only three digits.

q.q: A booking is for groups of 5 to 20 people. Which validation rule would wrongly reject groups of exactly 5 and 20?
o: Between 5 And 20
q.why: > and < exclude the limits. Between is inclusive, and >=5 And <21 accepts every whole number from 5 to 20.

q.q: In an Access input mask, what does the character 9 mean?
o: A digit is required in that position
A letter is required in that position
Any character may go in that position
A digit is optional in that position
q.why: L = letter required, 0 = digit required, 9 = digit optional.

q.q: Which validation rule and validation text pair is correct for an exam mark?
o: Len([ExamMark])=100 with 'Marks must be from 0 to 100'
Is Not Null with 'Marks must be from 0 to 100'
>0 And <100 with 'Marks must be from 0 to 100'
Between 0 And 100 with 'Marks must be from 0 to 100'
q.why: Between is inclusive, matching the text. >0 And <100 would reject 0 and 100; Len counts characters.

q.q: Which comparison operator means 'not equal to'?
q.why: <> means not equal, e.g. Size <> "M" returns everything except M.

q.q: Which criteria mean exactly the same as DailyRate BETWEEN 15 AND 22?
o: DailyRate > 15 AND DailyRate < 22
DailyRate >= 15 AND DailyRate <= 22
DailyRate >= 15 OR DailyRate <= 22
DailyRate > 15 OR DailyRate < 22
q.why: BETWEEN includes both end values, so it uses >= and <= joined by AND.

q.q: Why does the query Type = "Road" AND Type = "Electric" return no records?
o: Text criteria cannot be combined using AND
AND always returns every record in the table
Text values must be written between hash signs
One bike cannot be both types at once, so OR is needed
q.why: AND needs both conditions true for the same record, which is impossible on one field here.

q.q: How should a date be written in Access query criteria?
o: Between quotation marks, e.g. "01/06/2026"
Between hash signs, e.g. #01/06/2026#
Between square brackets, e.g. [01/06/2026]
With no symbols at all, e.g. 01/06/2026
q.why: Access puts dates between hash signs. Quotation marks are used for text.

q.q: A query uses the criterion "Mountain Bike" but the stored value is "Mountain". What happens?
o: It matches, because the first word of the value is the same
It does not match, because values must be typed exactly as stored
It matches every record whatever its type is
It causes the query to delete the matching record
q.why: Criteria must match the stored value exactly.

q.q: Which criterion would find all records with a DailyRate of £25 or more?
o: DailyRate > 25
DailyRate <= 25
DailyRate <> 25
DailyRate >= 25
q.why: 'Or more' includes 25 itself, so >= is needed; > 25 would leave out £25.

q.q: In the SQL query SELECT BikeID, Type FROM Bikes WHERE Size = 'M', which part chooses which records are returned?
o: WHERE Size = 'M'
SELECT BikeID, Type
FROM Bikes
ORDER BY BikeID
q.why: WHERE holds the criteria; SELECT chooses fields, FROM names the table and ORDER BY sorts.

q.q: A Bikes table has B01 Road M £18, B02 Mountain L £22, B03 Hybrid S £15, B04 Mountain M £25, B05 Electric L £35, B06 Hybrid M £15. Which records does DailyRate >= 25 OR Size = "S" return?
q.why: B03 is size S; B04 (£25) and B05 (£35) meet >= 25. With OR, one true condition is enough.

q.q: A Bikes table has B01 Road M £18, B02 Mountain L £22, B03 Hybrid S £15, B04 Mountain M £25, B05 Electric L £35, B06 Hybrid M £15. Which records does Type = "Hybrid" AND DailyRate > 15 return?
o: No records
q.why: Both hybrids cost exactly £15, and > 15 excludes 15, so nothing meets both conditions.

q.q: A Bikes table has B01 Road M £18, B02 Mountain L £22, B03 Hybrid S £15, B04 Mountain M £25, B05 Electric L £35, B06 Hybrid M £15. Which records does Size = "M" AND DailyRate < 20 return?
q.why: The size M bikes are B01, B04 and B06; B04 at £25 fails < 20.

q.q: A Bikes table has B01 Road M £18, B02 Mountain L £22, B03 Hybrid S £15, B04 Mountain M £25, B05 Electric L £35, B06 Hybrid M £15. Which records does Size <> "M" return?
q.why: <> "M" returns every record whose size is not M: the L and S bikes.

q.q: A Bikes table has B01 Road M £18, B02 Mountain L £22, B03 Hybrid S £15, B04 Mountain M £25, B05 Electric L £35, B06 Hybrid M £15. Which records does DailyRate BETWEEN 15 AND 22 return?
q.why: BETWEEN includes both ends, so £15 and £22 count as well as £18.

q.q: A Bikes table has B01 Road M £18, B02 Mountain L £22, B03 Hybrid S £15, B04 Mountain M £25, B05 Electric L £35, B06 Hybrid M £15. Which records does Type = "Mountain" OR Size = "L" return?
q.why: B02 and B04 are Mountain; B05 is size L. B02 meets both but is listed once.

q.q: A Bikes table has B01 Road M £18, B02 Mountain L £22, B03 Hybrid S £15, B04 Mountain M £25, B05 Electric L £35, B06 Hybrid M £15. Which records does DailyRate > 15 AND DailyRate < 25 return?
q.why: £18 and £22 lie strictly between the limits; £15 and £25 are excluded by > and <.

q.q: Which is the best definition of big data?
o: Data sets so large, fast-arriving and varied that ordinary database software cannot handle them
Any database table that contains more than one thousand records about its customers
Data that is stored together in a single very large flat-file table on one server
Data that has been compressed so it fits on one computer's storage drive
q.why: Big data is too big, too fast and too varied for ordinary tools to store or analyse in reasonable time.

q.q: Which V of big data describes the huge amount of data?
o: Volume
Velocity
Variety
Value
q.why: Volume is amount (terabytes or petabytes); velocity is speed; variety is different types.

q.q: A bank checks each card payment for fraud in under a second. Which V does this illustrate?
o: Volume
Variety
Velocity
Veracity
q.why: Velocity is the speed at which data is created and must be processed, often in real time.

q.q: A smart traffic system collects camera video, GPS locations and sensor counts. Which V does this illustrate?
o: Velocity
Volume
Variety
Value
q.why: Variety means many different types and formats of data, not a large amount.

q.q: Why must big data often be spread across many servers?
o: Each server can only hold one type of data
There is too much data to fit on one computer
Each record must be kept on its own server
Servers can only store structured data
q.why: The volume is too great for one computer, so it is spread across many servers, often in the cloud.

q.q: Which of these is structured data?
o: Teacher comments written in pupil reports
A table of exam marks with set data types
CCTV footage from a school car park
Voice notes recorded by a hospital doctor
q.why: Structured data fits a fixed format of fields and records. The others have no fixed format.

q.q: Why is structured data easy to search?
o: It is usually smaller than unstructured data
It is stored as images and video files
It needs AI tools to interpret its meaning
Every item sits in a known place in fields and records
q.why: A fixed format means ordinary queries such as Mark >= 70 can find data.

q.q: A spreadsheet of numbers is not stored in a database. Is it structured or unstructured data?
o: Structured, because it follows a fixed format
Unstructured, because it is not in a database
Unstructured, because it holds only numbers
Structured, because it is stored in the cloud
q.why: What matters is whether the data follows a fixed format, not which program holds it.

q.q: Which statement about big data is correct?
o: Most big data is structured
Unstructured data is easy to query
Big data never includes free text
Most big data is unstructured
q.why: Emails, posts, photos and video make up most big data, which is why it has high variety.

q.q: What is data mining?
o: Searching very large data sets to discover patterns nobody knew were there
Typing large amounts of data into a database by hand from forms
Deleting old and unused data to free up space on the servers
Checking data with validation rules as it is being entered
q.why: Data mining is part of data analytics: finding unknown patterns in very large data sets.

q.q: A health trust analyses A&E arrivals by hour, the weather and local events. What decision is this most likely to support?
o: Blocking unusual card payments as possible fraud
Recommending programmes to each viewer
Planning staff rotas for predicted busy periods
Changing the timings of traffic lights
q.why: The data predicts busy periods, so the trust can plan staffing.

q.q: Which reason links the variety of big data to the need for data analytics?
o: There is far too much of it for people to read
New data keeps arriving, so analysis must be fast
Much of it is unstructured, so simple queries cannot interpret it
It is all stored in tables that are hard to link
q.why: Variety means many unstructured types such as text, images and speech, needing tools such as AI. The other true statements relate to volume and velocity.

q.q: As well as specialist software, what does data analytics need?
o: Powerful processing and skilled data analysts
A single spreadsheet and a fast typist
A presence check on every single field
A full backup run on every night
q.why: Analytics needs powerful processing, often rented from the cloud, and analysts to ask the right questions.
